title: BIS Issues Rule Addressing Remote Access to American Super Intelligence Technology

quotes.text: Today, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released an interim final rule (IFR)—written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council—to address remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers.

The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.
November 15, 2026
quotes.for: The date printed on the downloadable announcement.

title: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors

quotes.text: First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau.

The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.

Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.
Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced.
This rule is effective [INSERT DATE OF PUBLICATION IN THE FEDERAL REGISTER].
License applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

You may not knowingly export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) items specified in paragraph (a) of § 744.24 for use in a data center to or within any destination worldwide that will provide access to more than 12,000,000 “aggregate TPP”
quotes.for: Threshold for the data center control.

withdrawn.why: The quoted preamble passage spells the term "in-county", not "in-country"; replaced with an exact passage from the operative threshold provision.

quotes.text: Foreign data centers will be expected to perform robust due diligence on their customers to identify direct or indirect ownership or control by Country Group D:5 or Macau persons.

The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met.

The prohibitions under § 744.24 do not apply when the computing power access is being provided exclusively for a ‘commercial recommender system’ under the (b)(2) exception provided the reporting requirements described therein are followed.
quotes.for: The exemption is specific to the new control, exclusive use and reporting.

quotes.text: This term does not include any SI system designed or used to generate novel text, image, audio, video, software, or other content in response to user inputs, or any system that incorporates such model, regardless of whether the system also performs recommendation functions.
quotes.for: Generative systems do not qualify as commercial recommender systems.

quotes.text: The notification from the exporter, reexporter, or transferor must also specify that the transferor, e.g., the data center operator, must obtain authorization for this change in end-use.
quotes.for: A subsequent change to a covered end-use requires authorization.

title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

quotes.text: The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.
quotes.for: An approximate scale for the threshold.
